metadata.name: free
metadata.description: Display amount of free and used memory in the system

installation.note: free is part of procps package, typically pre-installed on Ubuntu systems

overview.summary: The free command displays information about system memory usage, including total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory. It's essential for monitoring system resources and diagnosing memory-related issues.
when_to_use: Check if system needs more RAM

syntax.description: Display memory information. By default shows output in kilobytes with human-readable option available.

options.description: Display output in human-readable format (KB, MB, GB)
options.use_case: Easier to read output with automatic unit conversion
For systems with large amounts of RAM

options.description: Continuously display memory usage, updating every SECONDS
Display a line showing column totals
options.use_case: See total memory across all categories

examples.title: Basic memory information
examples.output:
total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:        8192000     2048000     1024000      512000     5120000     4608000
Swap:       2097152           0     2097152

elements.meaning: Memory currently in use by applications
Unused memory (not available for immediate use)
Memory used by kernel buffers and page cache (can be freed if needed)
Memory available for new processes (free + buff/cache that can be freed)
Virtual memory on disk (used when RAM is full)

output_explanation.notes: The 'available' column is the most important - it shows memory that can actually be used by new applications. 'free' is misleading as Linux uses free RAM for caching.

examples.use_case: Quick check of system memory status

common_misconceptions.title: Free memory is wasted
common_misconceptions.misconception: If free memory is low, the system is running out of memory
common_misconceptions.reality: Linux uses free RAM for disk caching (buff/cache) to improve performance. Low 'free' is normal and good - check 'available' instead.
common_misconceptions.tip: Look at 'available' column, not 'free' - it shows memory that can actually be used

common_misconceptions.title: High buff/cache is bad
common_misconceptions.misconception: High buff/cache means memory is being wasted
common_misconceptions.reality: buff/cache is memory used for disk caching, which significantly speeds up system performance. It's automatically freed when applications need memory.
common_misconceptions.tip: High buff/cache is actually a sign of efficient memory usage

common_pitfalls.description: Not checking if swap is being used, which indicates memory pressure
common_pitfalls.solution: Monitor swap usage - if it's being used, consider adding more RAM or optimizing memory usage

common_pitfalls.description: Using 'free' column to determine available memory
common_pitfalls.solution: Always check the 'available' column which accounts for cache that can be freed

best_practices: Use -h flag for human-readable output in daily use
Check swap usage - active swap indicates memory pressure
Use -s for continuous monitoring when diagnosing memory issues
Compare memory usage before and after running applications
performance_tips: If 'available' memory is consistently low, consider adding more RAM
High swap usage (swap used > 0) indicates system is under memory pressure
Monitor memory trends over time to identify memory leaks
Use free with watch for continuous monitoring: watch -n 1 free -h

related_commands.description: top provides detailed per-process memory information, while free shows system-wide totals
htop provides an interactive view of memory usage with per-process details
vmstat provides additional memory statistics including swap activity and memory pressure indicators

additional_notes.note1: The 'available' memory calculation was improved in newer versions of free to better reflect memory that can actually be used
additional_notes.note2: On systems with swap, free shows both RAM and swap memory separately
additional_notes.note3: For production monitoring, consider using monitoring tools like Prometheus or Nagios instead of manual free checks
